ta-l1d41q1-d1e100.summary: A divisio textus for Distinction 41. Lombard treats the causality of predestination and reprobation, excluding the error of those who placed their cause on our side: he shows neither has a cause on our part, excluding the view that our works as foreknown cause them (supported by an Augustinian text Lombard shows Augustine retracted, and a second retracted text that some try insufficiently to solve) and the view that prior works in reality cause them. He then shows that God's knowledge never diminishes, asking whether God always knows what he once knew or foreknew, answering first for foreknowledge and then for knowledge, with an objection and solution. Five articles are announced: whether election belongs to God eternally; the order of predestination to election; whether foreknowledge of merits causes predestination and reprobation; whether predestination is helped by the merits and prayers of the saints; and whether God now knows all he once knew.
claims: Predestination and reprobation have no cause on our part.
God's knowledge never diminishes.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e137.summary: First argument that there is no election in God. Election follows counsel as its conclusion (the Philosopher), and counsel is an inquiry, and inquiring knowledge does not fit God.
claims: Election follows inquiring counsel.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e140.summary: Second argument. Election implies discrimination, but God relates equally to all, as Dionysius says that as the sun, not reasoning or choosing, pours its rays on all bodies, so divine goodness on all creatures.
claims: God, like the sun, does not choose.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e146.summary: Third argument. Election requires a multitude among those chosen, and from eternity all were one in God, so election is not eternal, and whatever is in God is eternal.
claims: Eternal unity excludes election.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e150.summary: Fourth argument. Something in the chosen thing is understood to pre-exist the chooser's operation, but nothing in the creature pre-exists divine operation.
claims: Nothing pre-exists God's operation.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e153.summary: Sed contra from Eph. 1:4, 'he chose us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy'.
claims: God chose us before creation.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e159.summary: Thomas's determination. Election implies segregation, which can be only of things having some mixture or agreement, so there is no election of what is determined and distinct in itself; so election is not of the last end, naturally determined for each, but of means, by many of which the end can be reached, the more suitable being chosen (Ethics 3). Segregation can be in an operator's conception or in the execution of the work. From this: election does not belong to God regarding himself, since it is not of the end but of means; those chosen are chosen from those naturally apt to share the same end, so humans chosen for glory are chosen from humans, not from irrational beings; and election is eternal as in God's purpose, since he willed from eternity to segregate good from evil for glory, and temporal as in execution, as when someone is segregated from original or actual sin into grace, or from the common state into an office of prelacy, and other special divine gifts.
claims: Election is segregation among things agreeing in nature, of means, not of the end.
God's election is eternal in purpose and temporal in execution.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e162.summary: Reply to the first argument. Following inquiry is incidental to election, belonging to natures that know means only by inquiry, as we do, which does not fit God, who knows all with certainty.
claims: Inquiry is incidental to election.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e165.summary: Reply to the second argument. Though God in himself relates equally to all, not all have the same aptitude to receive his goodness, and he knows and orders this diversity, so election fits him. Dionysius's sun comparison concerns the universality of communication, not the lack of election: as the sun withholds its rays from none, God withholds his gifts from none, though they are not received alike in all, and God knows and orders this diversity, which the bodily sun does not.
claims: God gives to all but knows and orders their unequal reception.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e168.summary: Reply to the third argument. From eternity God knew not only the being things had in him but the being they would have in their own nature, in which they are not one but greatly distant in participating divine goodness, so election belongs to him eternally.
claims: God eternally knows things' diverse natural being.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e172.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Nothing in the thing pre-exists the operation of creation, so what is brought into being is not properly said to be chosen, but nature pre-exists, in its own being or in divine knowledge, the operation by which God justifies and glorifies.
claims: Election presupposes nature, not creation.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e184.summary: First argument that election does not conceptually precede predestination. Election adds to foreknowledge an act of will (the Philosopher), and predestination adds to foreknowledge only the will of some people's salvation, so they are the same.
claims: Both add will to foreknowledge.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e187.summary: Second argument. Election presupposes diversity among those chosen, and human diversity in attaining the end comes from predestination's effect, grace, so election follows predestination.
claims: Diversity comes from grace.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e190.summary: Third argument. Calling follows predestination (Rom. 8:30), and calling seems the same as election, since what is chosen for something is called to it.
claims: Calling follows predestination.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e197.summary: Sed contra. Love (dilectio) presupposes election, as the name shows, and predestination follows love, since goods are prepared only for those loved.
claims: Dilectio implies electio.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e200.summary: Thomas's determination. Predestination and election add to foreknowledge, as disposition and providence do, so that as disposition and providence concern all things, election and predestination concern humans, and as providence adds to disposition, predestination adds to election (Dist. 40). Disposition concerns the ordering of the universe's parts to one another and to the end, one nature preferred to another by divine wisdom; likewise election is the divine ordering by which some are preferred to others for attaining beatitude. Providence concerns conferring what brings things to their end and applying them to it; likewise predestination concerns preparing for the elect the goods of grace and glory by which they are applied to the end. Usage confirms this: things are disposed, but both things and what is conferred on them are provided; likewise election is properly of humans, but predestination of humans and what is conferred on them, since grace is not said to be chosen for someone but predestined for him.
claims: Election is to predestination as disposition to providence: preference for beatitude, then preparation of grace and glory.
Election conceptually precedes predestination.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e203.summary: Reply to the first argument. Election is not an act of will absolutely but in order to the ordering intellect (the Philosopher); predestination says the act of will absolutely following that order. Divine election orders some to beatitude by his wisdom; predestination prepares for them what leads to the end; so as the will ordering to the end precedes the act of will preparing the means, election precedes predestination.
claims: Election orders to the end; predestination prepares means.
concepts: will ordering end vs. preparing means

ta-l1d41q1-d1e206.summary: Reply to the second argument. Divine election does not presuppose diversity of grace, which follows it, but diversity of nature in divine knowledge, and it makes diversity of grace, as disposition makes diversity of nature.
claims: Election makes diversity of grace.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e209.summary: Reply to the third argument. Calling is always temporal, implying a leading to something. There is a calling to being by creation, to which no eternal election corresponds (Rom. 4:17, 'who calls the things that are not as things that are'), and a temporal calling to grace, to which temporal and eternal election correspond, interior by infusion of grace or exterior by a preacher's voice. Interior calling and temporal election to grace are always simultaneous but differ conceptually, election as segregation regarding the starting point and calling more the end point; calling differs conceptually from justification, since it pertains to the motion of nature toward grace, while justification regards the being following the motion's term, as grace makes one just. How love relates to election and predestination belongs to Book III, Dist. 32.
claims: Calling is temporal, interior or exterior; it differs conceptually from election and justification.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e225.summary: First argument that foreknowledge of merits causes predestination. Ambrose's Gloss on Rom. 9 has God say 'I will give grace to him whom I know will return to me with his whole heart after error', and the purpose of giving grace is predestination.
claims: God gives grace to those foreknown to return.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e231.summary: Second argument. God's predestining will cannot be unjust, and distributive justice gives unequal things only to the unequal, and humans are unequal for grace only by their or others' works, since all have natural capacity for grace.
claims: Distributive justice requires inequality of merit.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e234.summary: Third argument. In foreknowledge of works there is the eternal (God's knowledge) and the temporal (the works); in predestination the eternal (God's will) and the temporal (giving grace). The eternal in foreknowledge is conceptually prior to and in a way the cause of that in predestination, since will presupposes knowledge, and the temporal causes the temporal in a way, since the work preparing for grace is a material disposition and the work informed by grace a meritorious cause of glory.
claims: Foreknowledge precedes will; works dispose to and merit grace and glory.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e238.summary: Fourth argument. Predestination presupposes election, and one is chosen over another only for greater aptitude for the end, which can only be greater preparation for grace through works.
claims: Election requires greater aptitude.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e241.summary: Fifth argument. Predestination is the will for someone's salvation, not antecedent will, by which God wills all to be saved (Damascene), but consequent will, which regards merits.
claims: Consequent will regards merits.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e244.summary: Sed contra. What regards merit is in some way owed, not wholly gratuitous, and predestination is of gratuitous will, which no merits call forth (Augustine).
claims: Predestination is gratuitous.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e247.summary: Second sed contra: everything adduced in the text points the same way.
claims: Lombard's authorities deny merit as cause.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e250.summary: Thomas's determination. Foreknowledge of merits or works is in no way a cause of divine predestination, considering all that is of its essence, but nothing prevents its effect, grace and glory, placed obliquely in its definition, from having some cause in our operations. Of predestination's essence are foreknowledge and will of some people's salvation. God's knowledge of their salvation is not caused by knowledge of any works, since he does not know effects through causes but through himself: he does not know this because he knows its cause, but beholding his essence, the likeness of all, he sees each in itself, cause and caused. His will, freer than any, has no cause but its end, his goodness, which is himself, so God wills this for his goodness, not because he knows it or it was done. But the effect of his will, the thing willed as ordered to his goodness, can proceed from a cause God foreknew eternally, and he wills this order of cause to effect, willing the effect to be because the cause is, the causality referring not to the willing but to the willed; this cause of the willed, not of the willing, is called a reason of the will on the side of the effect. Such a cause sometimes has the complete character of cause and sufficiently produces the effect, sometimes is only a disposition. So our operation relates differently to predestination's two effects: a meritorious work informed by grace is the meritorious cause of glory, but a good work preceding grace is not its meritorious cause, only a disposition. So predestination has no cause but has a reason on the side of the effect, by which it is called rational and just.
claims: Foreknowledge of merits does not cause predestination, whose essence is God's knowledge and free will, caused by nothing but his goodness.
God wills that glory follow merit and grace follow disposition: causes of the willed, not of the willing.
Works informed by grace merit glory; works before grace only dispose to it.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e253.summary: Reply to the first argument. Ambrose does not mean our work causes the divine will or the giving of grace, but only disposes to it, and of the preceding work, not the subsequent one, which has its merit from grace. God purposes to infuse grace in one he foreknows will prepare himself, not because of the preparation, which is neither sufficient cause of grace nor end of his will, but because of his goodness; yet he wills that this person have grace because he prepared himself, as one says he gives grace because he prepared himself, the 'because' denoting disposition, not cause. With respect to the act of willing it denotes neither: he did not will because this person prepared, but only because it is good.
claims: 'Because he prepared himself' denotes disposition, not cause, and not of God's willing.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e257.summary: Reply to the second argument. Even in a just human the cause eliciting the act of willing is the will's end, but on the side of the effect it takes a cause from people's works, which distinguish them: asked why he gives more to one than another, a just judge would give the cause of his will, the good of justice shining in this work, or the cause of the work, that this person is more worthy. Regarding its last effect, glory, predestination has the character of distributive justice, so God gives glory to one and not another because one merits and not the other, and wills it because one is worthy. Regarding its first effect, grace, it has rather the character of liberality than justice, since grace is given gratis, not rendered to merits, so on the recipient's side no cause of worthiness for grace can be assigned, only some disposition.
claims: Glory follows distributive justice; grace follows liberality.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e260.summary: Reply to the third argument. Foreknowledge is not the cause of will, since will is free and I can not will what I know, so the argument fails, since only its end elicits the act of will.
claims: Knowledge does not cause free willing.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e263.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. Divine election requires diversity among the elect, not as causing the choosing will, but rather the reverse, as his disposition causes the diversity of natures.
claims: Election causes, not presupposes, diversity of grace.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e266.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. Consequent will is included in the concept of predestination, regarding works not as cause of the will but as meritorious cause of glory and preparation for grace.
claims: Consequent will regards works as causes of the effects.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e278.summary: First argument that predestination is not helped by any human work. A cause that produces its effect by itself is more perfect than one that is helped, and predestination is the most perfect cause.
claims: The most perfect cause needs no help.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e281.summary: Second argument. What leaves the effect unchanged whether posited or removed does not help, and the predestined will be saved whether prayed for or not, since predestination cannot fail.
claims: Prayer seems idle for the predestined.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e284.summary: Third argument. The effects of predestination, grace and glory, are from God alone.
claims: Grace and glory are from God alone.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e288.summary: Sed contra. Gregory says predestination is helped by the saints' prayers, as Isaac prayed for barren Rebecca and she conceived (Gen. 25), and Jacob, born of that conception, was predestined to life.
claims: Isaac's prayer helped predestination.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e291.summary: Second sed contra. If predestination is not helped by our works, we need not pray for others or ourselves or do good works, and the divine law urging good works would be vain.
claims: Otherwise prayer and works would be vain.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e294.summary: Third sed contra. Natural powers and gratuitous habits would be in vain, since we would not need to act to attain the end.
claims: Otherwise powers and habits would be vain.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e297.summary: Thomas's determination. This depends on the previous article: predestination is helped as it has a cause. As a divine act, willing or knowing, it has no cause on our side and so no help, since God performs the act of willing with no creature cooperating. But its effect is helped as it has causes, so every cause by whose intervening operation predestination's effect is completed is said to help predestination: as meritorious cause, condignly (one in grace merits eternal life by his act) or congruously (one praying for another merits first grace for him, or persuades him to good: 'we are God's helpers', 1 Cor. 3:9); as disposition (one preparing himself for grace); or by natural operation, as the heavens' motion and all natural causes help predestination, by whose service the elect are generated and sustained.
claims: Predestination as God's act has no help; its effect is helped by merit (condign or congruous), disposition, and natural causes.
Prayer for others can merit first grace congruously.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e303.summary: Reply to the first argument. This help is not because predestination needs it but to preserve the order divine wisdom established in things, that effects proceed from the first cause through secondary causes.
claims: Secondary causes preserve the order of wisdom.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e306.summary: Reply to the second argument. The argument assumes a falsehood: if Stephen had not prayed for his persecutors, Paul perhaps would not have been saved, as one who did not do meritorious works would not receive the crown predestined for him. Yet predestination cannot be frustrated, since God foreknew that this person would be saved by such a cause and order, so as it is incompossible with predestination that he not be saved, so it is incompossible that he not have been prayed for, though each is in itself possible not to be.
claims: Predestination includes its means, such as others' prayers.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e310.summary: Reply to the third argument. God alone infuses grace, but disposition to grace can come from the recipient himself, congruous merit of grace from another just person, and condign merit of grace from the man Christ, whose merits are effective for all human nature, since he is head of the Church.
claims: Christ merits grace condignly as head of the Church.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e322.summary: First argument that God now knows whatever he once knew. God's knowledge is invariable, and knowledge that ceases to be of what it was of varies.
claims: Invariable knowledge cannot lose objects.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e325.summary: Second argument. What God knows is a thing or an enuntiable signifying the thing's being; he knows now any thing he knew, since the same thing is now present, was future, and will be past, and there seems one truth, since an enuntiable's truth reduces to the thing's as cause.
claims: One thing, one truth.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e328.summary: Third argument. Co-signification relates more closely to a word than to a sentence, and different modes of signifying do not destroy a name's unity ('albus, alba, album' is one name), so 'Socrates runs' and 'Socrates ran', referred to one instant but said at different times, differ only in co-signified time and are one enuntiable.
claims: Tense differences are like inflection.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e332.summary: Fourth argument. Either unity of time pertains to the enuntiable's unity, and then these refer to one time and are one, or not, and then they differ only by co-signified time and are one.
claims: Dilemma on time and unity.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e335.summary: Fifth argument. An enuntiable is a thing of reason, and God knows whatever thing he knew.
claims: Enuntiables are things of reason.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e338.summary: Sed contra. Everything known by God is true, and it was once true that Christ would die, so it was known by God.
claims: 'Christ will die' was once known.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e341.summary: Second sed contra. Whatever is known by God is true, and it is not now true that Christ will die, so it is not known now; so not whatever God knew he knows.
claims: 'Christ will die' is no longer true.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e344.summary: Third sed contra, against the reply that the reasoning commits the fallacy of figure of speech, changing 'what' into 'when'. The difficulty remains, since one can say 'not every enuntiable God knew he knows', and an enuntiable is something known.
claims: The fallacy reply does not remove the difficulty.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e347.summary: Thomas's determination. God's knowledge is of enuntiables as well as things (Dist. 38). Referred to things, he undoubtedly knows every thing he knew, and Lombard's solution is excellent, since the same thing is signified when 'Socrates runs' and 'Socrates ran' are said at different times, Socrates' running. Referred to enuntiables, there were two opinions. Some said unity of the thing signified gives unity of the enuntiable even with different co-signified time, so an enuntiable once true is always true and what God once knew he always knows. This contradicts the Philosopher (Categories), who says the same proposition, 'Socrates sits', true while he sits, becomes false when he rises; and if enuntiables took unity from the thing, they would take diversity from diversity, so 'Socrates runs' said at different times would not be one, nor would any name signifying different things be one, destroying both equivocation and univocation, which require one name for many. So all moderns grant 'Socrates runs' and 'Socrates ran' are two enuntiables even referring to the same running. So the enuntiable can be taken materially, as a thing of reason, and then God knows whatever enuntiable he knew, since he always knows 'Socrates runs' has such a nature and parts; or significatively, as designating the thing's being with conditions given by the verb's co-signification, and then not whatever enuntiable God knew he knows: he knew 'Christ is crucified' to be true when he was crucified, but now knows it not to be true but to have been true.
claims: God knows every thing he knew, but not every enuntiable taken significatively, since tensed enuntiables change in truth.
'Socrates runs' and 'Socrates ran' are different enuntiables even about one event.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e351.summary: Reply to the first argument. This comes not from change in God's knowledge but in the thing. As 'God foreknew Christ would die' designates a relation to the future, so when it ceases to be future God no longer foreknows it, without change in his foreknowledge, so 'God knew Christ would die' designates a relation of future in the participle, and when the thing passes into the past the relation does not remain, so God does not know the thing to be under that relation. His knowledge, beholding all at one glance, does not vary; the relation in the thing's nature varies, since in relative predications one extreme can change while the other remains invariable.
claims: The change is in the thing's relation, not in God's knowledge.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e354.summary: Reply to the second argument. Though an enuntiable's truth is caused by the thing's being, unity of the thing gives it not unity but truth; it has unity and diversity from what essentially constitutes it, its parts, and since 'Socrates runs' and 'Socrates ran' have different parts, they are different enuntiables.
claims: Enuntiables are individuated by their parts.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e357.summary: Reply to the third argument. Different modes of signifying also make different names; grammarians call 'albus, alba, album' one name not because it is simply one, since they are several words, and multiplying the genus (word) multiplies the species (name), but because they belong to the same declension.
claims: Inflected forms are one name only by declension.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e360.summary: Reply to the fourth argument. The time signified is outside the enuntiable's essence, so it takes unity or diversity not from it but from the time co-signified, since different co-signified times give different verb endings, words, and enuntiables.
claims: Co-signified time individuates enuntiables.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e363.summary: Reply to the fifth argument. Taking the enuntiable as a thing, the argument holds, but that is beside the point.
claims: Materially taken, the argument holds.

ta-l1d41q1-d1e372.summary: An expositio textus. (1) 'But this is frivolous': the exposition that some are worthy of grace because they are not as unworthy as others is too contrived. (2) 'As the ancient fathers believed Christ would be born and die, we believe he was born and died': the diversity of enuntiables does not hinder the unity of the thing believed, since either the object of faith is the thing, not the enuntiable, as some say, or the enuntiable abstracting from every difference of time, determinate time not being of the substance of faith but coming to it as determined by teaching, since faith comes from hearing.
claims: The unity of faith across time rests on the thing believed or on a tenseless enuntiable.

ta-l1d41q1-Dd1e95.summary: The Prooemium of Distinction 41 divides Lombard's denial that predestination and reprobation have causes on our part and his account of the immutability of God's knowledge. It announces five articles: election, its order to predestination, merits as cause, helps to predestination, and whether God knows now all he knew.
claims: Predestination has no cause on our part.

ta-l1d41q1-Dd1e129.summary: Article 1 holds that election, segregation among things agreeing in nature and concerning means rather than the end, belongs to God eternally in purpose and temporally in execution. It requires no inquiry in God, and though God gives to all he knows and orders their unequal reception. He eternally knows things' diverse natural being, and election presupposes nature, not creation.
claims: God's election is eternal in purpose, temporal in execution.

ta-l1d41q1-Dd1e176.summary: Article 2 holds that election is to predestination as disposition to providence: God first prefers some for beatitude, then prepares grace and glory for them. So election conceptually precedes predestination and causes diversity of grace. Calling is temporal, interior or exterior, and conceptually distinct from election and justification.
claims: Election precedes predestination as disposition precedes providence.

ta-l1d41q1-Dd1e217.summary: Article 3 holds that foreknowledge of merits in no way causes predestination, whose essence, God's knowledge and free will, has no cause but his goodness. God wills that his effects follow from causes: works informed by grace merit glory, and works before grace only dispose to it. So predestination has a reason on the side of the effect. Glory follows distributive justice, and grace liberality.
claims: Merits do not cause predestination but are causes of its effects: glory merited, grace prepared for.
Grace is from liberality, glory from justice.

ta-l1d41q1-Dd1e270.summary: Article 4 holds that predestination as God's act is not helped, but its effect is helped by condign and congruous merit, by disposition, and by natural causes, preserving the order of secondary causes. Predestination includes its means, like others' prayers (Stephen for Paul), and Christ merits grace condignly as head of the Church.
claims: Prayers and merits help the effect of predestination, which includes them as means.

ta-l1d41q1-Dd1e314.summary: Article 5 holds that God knows every thing he once knew, but not every enuntiable taken significatively, since tensed enuntiables like 'Christ will die' change in truth. This change is in the thing's relation, not in God's knowledge. 'Socrates runs' and 'Socrates ran' are different enuntiables, individuated by their parts and co-signified time.
claims: God's knowledge does not change, though tensed enuntiables do.

ta-l1d41q1-Dd1e367.summary: The Expositio textus of Distinction 41 rejects a contrived exposition of worthiness for grace. It explains the unity of faith across times by the thing believed or by a tenseless enuntiable.
claims: Faith is one across time.

ta-l1d41q1.summary: Quaestio 1 of Book I, Distinction 41 treats the causes of predestination and the immutability of God's knowledge. Election is eternal in purpose and precedes predestination as disposition precedes providence. Foreknowledge of merits does not cause predestination, whose only cause is God's goodness, though God wills that grace-informed merits cause glory and preparation dispose to grace. Predestination's effect is helped by merit, prayer, disposition, and natural causes, which it includes as means. God knows every thing he once knew, though tensed enuntiables change in truth.
claims: Predestination has no cause in our merits but includes merits and prayers as causes of its effects.
Election precedes predestination.
God's knowledge is immutable though tensed propositions change.
